paras: The lynching of Bill Cater took place at Doe Run (also spelled Doerun), Georgia, in August 1900, when an armed mob of about fifty men forced its way into the town jail at night, took out Cater, a Black prisoner charged with attempted criminal assault on a white woman, and shot him to death. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story to papers across the country within two days, repeating the claim that Cater had confessed and been identified by the woman.

Cater was held on a charge of attempted criminal assault on a white woman, whom the Dawson News, a Georgia weekly, named as Mrs. Vickers. According to the wire dispatch, he confessed as soon as he was captured and was later identified by the woman; the claim reached print only through that dispatch, and no statement from Cater himself appears in the coverage.

The dispatch, dated Doe Run, August 18, said the mob came "last night", which places the attack on Friday, August 17. An armed mob "numbering fifty men forcibly entered the jail", took Cater out and "riddled him with bullets", and he died instantly. The Dawson News described the building as a "guard house" and said the fifty men "stormed" it on Friday night. None of the reports names a member of the mob or says what any jailer or officer did.
No report of an inquest, an arrest or a grand jury inquiry was found in the coverage.

The dispatch ran on August 19 in Louisville, Savannah, Richmond, Raleigh, Birmingham, Houston, St. Paul, Indianapolis and New York, and the next day in Portland, Maine, Rock Island and Wheeling. Weeklies picked it up later, from the Farmer and Mechanic and the Yorkville Enquirer to the County Record and the Democratic Advocate, and the Macon Beacon in Mississippi printed a two-line version on September 1. Most versions repeated the confession and identification without comment, and some went further: the Raleigh News and Observer dropped the word "attempted", and the Portland Daily Press said Cater "had confessed to criminally assaulting a white woman".

Headlines in several papers treated the charge as settled. The Savannah Morning News ran the story on its front page as "For the Usual Crime", the Wheeling Sunday Register as "Rape Fiend Lynched", the News and Observer as "Rapist Riddled With Balls" and the Saint Paul Globe as "Negroe's Usual Fate". Other papers used plainer heads, such as "Lynch Law In Georgia" in The Sun and "Another Lynching in Georgia" in the Rock Island Argus. In Georgia the Dawson News placed the item in its "Georgia Gleanings" column, and the Southern Christian Advocate's weekly summary recorded only that at Doerun a "negro [was] lynched for usual cause".
No coverage of the lynching was found in the Black press.

The papers disagreed on the night of the attack. The original dispatch of August 18 and the Dawson News pointed to Friday, and the Rock Island Argus said "Friday night", but the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, the Yorkville Enquirer and the County Record said Saturday night and the Democratic Advocate said Sunday night. The Friday date is the one that fits the earliest dispatch and the only Georgia account with details of its own.

The Yorkville Enquirer placed the lynching at "Darien, Ga.", although its brief otherwise matches the Doe Run dispatch. The victim's name also appeared as "Bill Carter" in the Wheeling Sunday Register and as "William Cater" in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer.

reader.title: Lynching of Bill Cater
bases: An armed mob forced its way into the jail at Doe Run, Georgia, took out Bill Cater, a Black prisoner charged with attempted assault, and shot him dead (A1, A4, A17).

Every account says a mob, numbered at fifty, took Cater from the jail and riddled him with bullets, killing him instantly (A1, A4, A17); the papers tie the killing to his being charged with attempted assault on a white woman, and the Dawson News calls it a lynching (A17).

Most papers ran a single Associated Press dispatch (A1, A4, A12), but the Georgia weekly Dawson News gave details absent from the wire, the 'guard house' and the woman's name, and agrees on the core event (A17).

accounts.label: Wire report (Associated Press)
accounts.gist: Fifty armed men forcibly entered the Doe Run jail 'last night', took out Cater and riddled him with bullets; he had been charged with attempted criminal assault, had confessed when captured and had been identified by the woman.

accounts.label: Georgia weekly (Dawson News)
accounts.gist: Fifty armed men stormed the guard house at Doerun on Friday night and lynched a Black man who, the paper said as fact, had attempted an assault on Mrs. Vickers.

framing.detail: Headlines treated the accusation as proved: 'For the Usual Crime' (Savannah), 'Rape Fiend Lynched' (Wheeling Sunday Register), 'Rapist Riddled With Balls' (Raleigh), 'Negroe's Usual Fate' (St. Paul).
Most papers printed the AP dispatch unchanged, repeating the claim of confession and identification without comment.
Some northern papers headed it as lynch law without endorsing the charge: 'Lynch Law In Georgia' (The Sun), 'Another Lynching in Georgia' (Rock Island).

versions.value: Friday night, Aug. 17 (AP dated Aug. 18, 'last night')

conflicts.note: Friday fits the original dispatch dated August 18 and the Georgia paper; the Saturday and Sunday versions appear in later briefs and weeklies and carry no other new detail.
The Yorkville brief otherwise matches the wire text; Darien is a single, unnamed variant.
The Georgia paper's term may describe the same lockup.
